claims.text: HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices initially show improved tribological performance as ambient temperature rises.
The initial improvement with temperature is caused by formation of a protective, self-healing oxide tribofilm that reduces friction and wear.
Above a critical temperature, tribological performance degrades because the tribofilm becomes unstable, softens, or spalls and the underlying alloy softens.
CoCrFeMnNi-family HEA coatings can be deposited on steel transition-metal substrates by plasma cladding or spray-based processes.
Laser-cladded CoCrBFeNiSi HEA coatings can have an amorphous structure.
HEA coatings in this class may be used in an as-deposited or heat-treated state.
An air environment during wear testing permits oxidation of the coating surface.
A mixed Cr2O3, Al2O3, and Fe2O3 tribofilm forms on the worn surface and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact.
The stability and mechanical properties of the oxide tribofilm depend on temperature.
At low to moderate temperatures, rapid formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer reduces friction, suppresses adhesive wear, and improves wear resistance.
Increasing temperature initially makes the tribofilm more protective and lowers the wear rate.
At approximately 400-500°C, the tribofilm may transform, coarsen, lose adhesion, and spall.
Elevated temperature may cause matrix softening, recrystallization, or precipitation of soft phases, thereby reducing coating hardness and wear resistance.
Wear rate will decline with temperature up to an optimum near 300-400°C and then rise sharply.
The friction coefficient will initially decrease because of tribofilm lubrication and then increase at high temperature because spalled oxide produces abrasive wear.
At room temperature, wear is dominated by adhesive and abrasive mechanisms without significant oxide formation.
For most HEA coatings, degradation begins above approximately 450-500°C because the tribofilm loses stability and the matrix softens.
Below -100°C, embrittlement and crack propagation may increase wear.
The degradation threshold depends on HEA composition, coating microstructure, load, speed, and environment.
Al, Cr, or Si additions can shift the optimum temperature range by promoting more stable oxide layers.

contradictions.description: The predicted wear-rate increase begins after an optimum at 300-400°C, the mechanism places the critical regime at 400-500°C, and the boundary says degradation occurs above 450-500°C; these ranges do not define one consistent onset.

The baseline says room-temperature wear occurs without significant oxide formation, while the mechanism attributes enhanced resistance at low to moderate temperatures to rapid formation of a dense oxide layer; whether room temperature belongs to that regime is unresolved.
